paras: The lynching of Sam Smith took place near Forney, Texas, on October 25, 1888, when armed and masked men took Smith, a Black man accused of rape, from officers taking him to jail at Kaufman and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown persons, and Black residents refused to let him be buried in their graveyard. Texas papers noted the speed of the killing, which came less than a day after the alleged crime.

On the afternoon of October 24, a man described as a "negro tramp" was accused of assaulting the wife of Henry Boyd, a section boss, at the section house east of Forney. According to the first Forney dispatch, he found her alone, drew a pistol, and then escaped on the evening train. He was arrested on the train between Mesquite and Dallas, a pistol was found on him, and he was jailed in Dallas.

On the morning of October 25, Constable P. E. Yates of Forney brought him back on the early train, arriving at 10 o'clock. Placed in a room with several other men, he was picked out by the woman, and, according to the correspondent, said he was the man but would never do so again if released. A crowd then raised "a great racket," demanding that he be handed over, with cries of "Hang him!" "Shoot him!" "Burn him!"

Once the crowd had quieted, officers started with him for the jail at Kaufman. About a mile out, at a small creek, "a body of armed and masked men" overpowered them, hanged him to a bois d'arc tree, and shot him several times.

'Squire I. S. Moore went to the site and held an inquest, whose jury found that Smith had died "at the hands of some unknown persons." His body was brought back to town and left exposed to view for about an hour before it was taken away. The "colored people" of Forney would not allow him to be buried in their graveyard, and the correspondent could not learn where he was buried. No report of arrests, a grand jury, or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Coverage came only from Texas white papers, all drawing on a Forney correspondent. The Fort Worth Daily Gazette ran the first report under the headline "Assaulted a White Woman" and the next day printed "The Particulars," which treated the rape charge as fact and called the hanging "one of the quickest punishments ever visited on a criminal in this county during the past dozen years." The San Antonio Daily Light reduced the story to two "State News" items on "the colored rapist, Sam Smith," set among notes on crops and the state fair.

A week later the Austin Weekly Statesman printed the same account as a Dallas special telegram headed "Lynch Law. A Negro Rapist Taken From the Officers and Hung." None of these papers questioned the accusation or criticized the lynchers.

The Gazette gave the time of the hanging as 1:10 o'clock, while the Statesman's otherwise identical text gave 11:10. The Gazette placed the section house about four miles east of Forney, and the Light two miles east.

accounts.label: Forney/Dallas correspondent
accounts.gist: After the woman identified him and he reportedly admitted it, officers started for Kaufman, and masked men overpowered them a mile out, hanged him and shot him.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death at the hands of some unknown persons.

framing.detail: The Gazette called him 'the negro who committed the rape' and the lynching 'one of the quickest punishments ever visited on a criminal'; the accusation is stated as fact throughout.
The San Antonio Light ran it as a one-line 'State News' item on 'the colored rapist, Sam Smith'.
The Austin Statesman ran the correspondent's account a week later under 'Lynch Law. A Negro Rapist Taken From the Officers and Hung.'
